newsitem.title: FALKLAND ISLANDS: UK will not weaken Falkland Islands defence.
newsitem.headline: UK will not weaken Falkland Islands defence.

text.p: British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo on Thursday told Falkland Islanders that the government would not weaken their defences against Argentina despite improving ties with Buenos Aires.

"The government is committed to defending the islands and maintaining their security. There is no caveat, exception or time limit to that commitment," Portillo said in a speech aimed at the 2,400 inhabitants of the South Atlantic islands.

Since fighting a brief war with Argentina over the Falklands in 1982 Britain has reinforced the bare, windswept islands with about 2,000 troops and built a huge military complex and airport on the site of a former sheep ranch.
Islanders say they are still nervous about Argentina's intentions despite the British defence build-up, which Portillo said had cost 3.6 billion pounds ($6 billion).

Portillo earlier said Britain was pleased by the conciliatory tone of recent statements by Argentine President Carlos Menem, whose government claims the archipelago, known in Argentina as the Malvinas.
But he rejected Menem's suggestion of the possibility of some kind of shared sovereignty over the islands.
"Britain has always made clear that sovereignty is not only not for sharing and not for surrendering but also not for discussion," Portillo told Reuters.
Argentine forces, acting on a long-standing sovereignty claim, seized the islands in 1982 but were dislodged 10 weeks later by a British task force. Argentina maintains its sovereignty demand.
But any suggestion Buenos Aires might tale over makes kelpers, as the islanders are known, bristle.
"No way. Never," said one sheep rancher.
"Most people are now confident of the British commitment," said the islanders' London-appointed governor, Richard Ralph.
"I don't think people feel they are under military threat. But they don't react well to reiterations by the Argentine government of its intentions to recover sovereignty by the year 2000," he said.

Once dependent on wool, the islands now bask in a rare prosperity thanks to the sale of fishing licenses to big foreign trawlers working nearby. Foreign oil companies are due to start full-scale exploration in late 1997.
